metadata.note: The Troy and Greenbush Railroad -- six miles down the east bank of the Hudson that mattered far out of proportion to their length. Incorporated May 14 1845 and finished on Jun 13 the same year, the line joined Troy to Greenbush, opposite Albany, and closed the last gap in an all-rail route from Boston to Buffalo. In the twenty years before Albany had a bridge, this was half of an awkward arrangement: passengers ferried across the river while their train ran north to Troy, crossed on the Rensselaer and Saratoga's covered bridge at Green Island, and came back down the west bank. The Hudson River Railroad leased the line from Jun 1 1851 and opened through to New York City that October; the Troy Union Railroad, opened 1854, sorted out the four-railroad tangle at the Troy end. The Livingston Avenue Bridge of 1866 finally let trains cross at Albany itself and ended the detour. The line passed to the New York Central and carried D&H Montreal trains into Troy Union Station until passenger service at Troy ended in January 1958.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:WikiProject_Trains/ICC_valuations/Troy_and_Greenbush_Railroad -- Interstate Commerce Commission, Valuation Reports vol. 27 (incorporated May 14 1845 by special act of the Legislature of New York to build from Troy to Greenbush; owned mileage 5.553 miles, the company's own figure 5.56; construction completed Jun 13 1845; operated by its own organization until Jun 1 1851 and by the New York Central and its predecessors under lease thereafter; leased to the New York Central for the term of its corporate existence from Jun 1 1851)

https://vizettes.com/kt/rr/cd-rr-history/index.htm -- The Growth of Railroads in the Capital District (the Troy and Greenbush of 1845 connected Troy south to East Albany, now Rensselaer, on the east side of the Hudson; before bridges, passengers crossed on ferries while the train went up to Troy, crossed the Hudson and came back down to Albany; the Hudson River Railroad extended the line to New York City by 1851)

https://www.newyorkalmanack.com/2025/09/albany-livingston-railroad-bridge/ and https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Livingston_Avenue_Bridge (the first engine crossed the Livingston Avenue Bridge Feb 18 1866 and passenger trains from Feb 22; the present bridge dates from 1901-2 on the 1866 pilings)

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_Station_(Troy,_New_York) (Troy Union Station, designed by Reed and Stem, served the New York Central, Boston and Maine and Delaware and Hudson; D&H Laurentian and Montreal Limited trains used NYC tracks into the station and transferred to D&H rails going north; the B&M Minute Man was cut back to Greenfield in January 1958, precipitating the station's closure and demolition that year)
metadata.not_yet_sourced: The traced 7.51 mi does not match the ICC's 5.553 miles of owned road and the difference is not resolved -- see geometry_quality. No timetable has been consulted, so every headway and speed is an estimate. January 1958 is the month passenger service at Troy ended, and it is dated to the Boston and Maine's cutback rather than to a last train over this particular six miles; when New York Central local service between Troy and Rensselaer itself stopped has not been established, and 1958 is used as the outer bound. The 1903 segment boundary is the opening of Troy Union Station, not a change in service. The Troy Union Railroad's own trackage through Troy, the Greenbush ferry, and the Livingston Avenue Bridge are described in the notes but not drawn.
metadata.line_label_audit: 2026-08-24: line labels normalised repo-wide to "<operating company>: <line name>" -- the company's common display name (legal suffixes dropped), then the line as a passenger would have known it, or its two terminals where the line carried no advertised name. properties.line: Troy and Greenbush: Troy – Greenbush (East Albany)
properties.speed_source: estimated: a six-mile riverbank line with a ferry connection at each end of the journey; unsourced

segments.note: Incorporated May 14 1845 by special act of the New York legislature and built the same summer -- construction completed Jun 13 1845 -- 5.553 miles down the east bank from Troy to Greenbush, opposite Albany. It closed the last gap in an all-rail route between Boston and Buffalo. Albany itself had no Hudson bridge yet: passengers crossed by ferry, while trains that needed the west bank ran north to Troy, over the Rensselaer and Saratoga's bridge at Green Island, and back down the other side. The company worked its own trains until Jun 1 1851. Frequency estimated/unsourced

properties.geometry_source: Real-traced from OpenStreetMap (ODbL) via Overpass: the surviving east-bank corridor, today CSX's Colonie Subdivision and Troy Industrial Track, shortest-pathed from Rensselaer (the old Greenbush) north to the furthest point still connected toward Troy. 273 points, 7.51 mi, median vertex spacing 21 m.
properties.geometry_quality: Real-traced, no straight-line legs; median vertex spacing 21 m, longest step 511 m, 5 steps over 300 m. MILEAGE DOES NOT MATCH THE COMPANY FIGURE and the difference is unresolved: the ICC gives the Troy & Greenbush 5.553 miles of owned road, while this trace is 7.51 mi. Cumulative 5.553 mi along the trace lands at -73.71324,42.72577, about 1.9 km short of the Troy Union Station site, which is consistent with the company owning only as far as the edge of Troy and reaching the station over Troy Union Railroad trackage from 1854 -- but that is inference, not a sourced boundary, and the excess may instead be later realignment. LATER ALIGNMENT: this is the corridor as it survives today, not a verified 1845 alignment. The last kilometre into the Troy Union Station site is lifted and sits in a disconnected fragment in OpenStreetMap, so the drawn line stops about 1 km short of where trains actually terminated.

properties.speed_source: estimated: 1850s-1860s Hudson River Railroad local service; unsourced

segments.note: Leased to the Hudson River Railroad from Jun 1 1851 at an annual rental of seven per cent on $275,000 of capital stock. The Hudson River Railroad, chartered May 12 1846, opened through to New York City on Oct 3 1851, so Troy gained a direct rail route down the east bank to the city. Congestion where four railroads met in Troy produced the Troy Union Railroad, organized 1851 and opened 1854, which carried the trains the last stretch into the union station. Frequency estimated/unsourced

segments.note: To the New York Central and Hudson River Railroad on the 1869 consolidation, and the lease was reaffirmed to the New York Central under the consolidation of 1913, running for the term of the Troy and Greenbush's corporate existence. The Livingston Avenue Bridge at Albany had opened in 1866 -- first engine Feb 18, passenger trains from Feb 22 -- so trains no longer had to detour through Troy to change banks. Frequency estimated/unsourced

segments.note: Troy Union Station, designed by Reed and Stem before their work on Grand Central, opened in 1903. The Delaware and Hudson's Laurentian and Montreal Limited came into it over New York Central tracks from the south before transferring to D&H rails northward. Passenger service at Troy ended in January 1958 when the Boston and Maine cut the Minute Man back to Greenfield, Massachusetts, and the station was demolished later that year. Frequency estimated/unsourced
